description: Hi, we’re Amigos from Palestine, led by Amir Almasri. Our interests include computer and biomedical engineering, hardware, chip and IC design, PCBs, robotics, and space health. We’re excited to bring together people who enjoy research, data analysis, software, hardware, design, and science communication to explore how engineering and medicine can address challenges in space.
summary:
AMIGOS: an offline health self-check for crews far from Earth

AMIGOS is a web app that lets an astronaut monitor their own health without internet or ground contact. A one-minute daily check-in covers sleep, food, water, mood and exercise. A Laboratory view records test results and signs and symptoms, and lets the crew untick tests their vehicle doesn’t carry. An Assessment view shows each result against published reference ranges, with NASA’s five spaceflight hazards (radiation, isolation, distance, gravity, hostile environment) as editable parameters for each spacecraft or location.

It addresses the challenge by turning the Human Research Program’s hazard research into plain-language next steps: self-care, run these tests, or contact the flight surgeon. It never diagnoses, and it never invents thresholds.

It matters because as missions go farther, delays reach 20 minutes each way and help takes longer. Crews need decision support that works on board. Our next step is a local AI model on the spacecraft server to analyse ECG and echo images.

That’s about 160 words. Two details are worth checking before you submit: the “20 minutes each way” figure comes from NASA’s hazards page, and the AI model is a proposed next step, not something the app does yet. The text says that clearly.
details:
AMIGOS is a web app with three views. In the Daily check-in, the crew answers about 20 simple questions (sleep, food, water, mood, exercise) and gets a short plan for the day. In the Laboratory, they log test results (blood pressure, heart rate, SpO₂, glucose and more) and tick signs and symptoms. In the Assessment, each result is compared with a published adult reference and drawn on a ring. The page also shows body systems, 7, 30 or 90-day trends, and NASA’s five spaceflight hazards as editable parameters for the spacecraft or location. A symptom leads to one of three plain-words outcomes: self-care, run these tests, or contact the flight surgeon now.

Benefits and intended impact

It works with no internet and no server. Data stays on the device, and each crew member sees only their own. One tool serves any vehicle, because tests the vehicle lacks are unticked and named, never counted as normal. The aim is to give crews on long missions, where messages can take up to 20 minutes each way, a quick, safe way to notice changes and know when to call a human.

Tools

HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript with no framework or build step. SVG for the charts. Browser storage (localStorage, and IndexedDB for imported files). An Excel research workbook, with a Python script that loads it into the app. GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting. AI tools (Claude) helped with code, source research and diagrams; the team reviewed the outputs.

Creativity

  • NASA’s hazards become live parameters beside the health results.
  • Symptoms choose which tests are worth running.
  • Sleep, mood, food, water and lab results sit on one timeline.
  • The research tables can be swapped without changing the screens.

What the team considered

  • Safety: The app never diagnoses and never invents a threshold. A strength of 4–5 always goes to a human.
  • Accessibility: Colours always come with icons and words.
  • Honesty: Demo data is separate from personal data, and placeholder or missing values are labelled “not loaded”.
  • Limits: The ranges are general adult references. The app has not been tested with a crew or reviewed by flight surgeons. A local AI model on the spacecraft server, to read ECG and echo images, is a planned improvement.
